title: Rousseau
orientation: Russell profiles Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712-1778) as a hugely influential 'social force' rather than a rigorous philosopher, tracing his disreputable biography before examining the two parts of his thought Russell considers philosophically significant: his invention of a heart-based, anti-rationalist theology, and his political theory of the Social Contract and the general will. The chapter matters because Russell treats Rousseau as the ancestor of a whole tradition -- running through Robespierre, Hegel, and into modern dictatorship -- that he sets against the Lockean liberal tradition represented by Roosevelt and Churchill.
historical_background: Rousseau was born in Calvinist Geneva in 1712, converted (opportunistically, by his own account) to Catholicism as a teenage runaway in Savoy, lived for years as a vagabond and dependent of patrons such as Madame de Warens, and rose to sudden fame with his prize-winning 1750 Discourse on the Arts and Sciences. His major works -- La Nouvelle Héloïse, Emile, and The Social Contract -- all appeared in 1760-1762; Emile and The Social Contract provoked official condemnation by the French government, the Sorbonne, and Geneva, forcing him into exile (including a period sheltered by Frederick the Great near Neuchâtel, and a stay in England with Hume that ended in a paranoid rupture). He died in Paris in 1778, in great poverty and amid suspicion of suicide, having by then developed a serious persecution mania.
philosophical_problems: Can religious belief be legitimately grounded in feeling ('the heart') rather than in intellectual argument?
What is the relationship between the individual's absolute surrender of rights in the social contract and genuine liberty?
What is the 'general will', and how, if at all, can it be identified in practice?
Can a doctrine that pays lip-service to democracy nonetheless justify totalitarian control by the State?
Is 'natural man', uncorrupted by civilization, a coherent or defensible ideal on which to found ethics and politics?

philosophers_discussed.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's sole primary subject: his biography, his theology of the heart (the 'Confession of Faith of a Savoyard Vicar'), and his political theory in The Social Contract (the social contract, the sovereign, the general will) are all examined in detail.

philosophers_discussed.name: Voltaire
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Rousseau's great rival and correspondent; quoted mocking the Discourse on Inequality ('One longs, in reading your book, to walk on all fours') and disputing with Rousseau over the Lisbon earthquake and the morality of theatre.

philosophers_discussed.name: David Hume
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Offered Rousseau refuge in England in 1762 and remained loyal longest, but was eventually suspected by Rousseau's persecution mania of plotting against him; Russell quotes Hume's sympathetic but damning final assessment of Rousseau's character.

philosophers_discussed.name: Edmund Burke
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Befriended Rousseau in England but their friendship cooled; quoted judging that Rousseau 'entertained no principle, either to influence his heart, or guide his understanding, but vanity.'

philosophers_discussed.name: John Locke
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Named as the founder of the rival tradition of political reform (Roosevelt and Churchill are said to descend from Locke, Hitler from Rousseau); Rousseau's social contract superficially resembles Locke's but proves closer to Hobbes's in substance, and Rousseau lacks Locke's respect for private property and division of powers.

philosophers_discussed.name: Thomas Hobbes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Rousseau's conception of the social contract, on inspection, is said to be more akin to Hobbes's than to Locke's, given its demand for total alienation of individual rights to the community.

schools_discussed: Natural religion / theology of the heart
Direct (City-State) democracy as theorized by Rousseau

core_concepts.name: Theology of the heart (natural religion)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Rousseau's innovation of basing belief in God not on logical proofs but on feelings -- the sense of awe at nature, the conviction that one simply cannot help believing. As he tells an aristocratic lady, doubt vanishes when he watches the sunrise.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A mode of religious justification, invented by Rousseau and later adopted by the majority of Protestant theologians, which grounds belief in God's existence in an aspect of human nature (emotion, conscience, aspiration) rather than in intellectual demonstration such as the ontological, cosmological, or design arguments.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell calls it a genuine historical innovation: before Rousseau, every philosopher who believed in God, from Plato onward, offered intellectual arguments for that belief; Rousseau is the first to substitute feeling for argument, a move that became so familiar its originality is easily missed.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out most formally in 'The Confession of Faith of a Savoyard Vicar', an interlude in Book IV of Emile (1762).
examples: 'I believe in God as strongly as I believe any other truth, because believing and not believing are the last things in the world that depend on me.'
The Savoyard Vicar finding moral rules 'in the depths of my heart, written by Nature in ineffaceable characters' rather than deducing them from philosophy
objections: The fact that Rousseau cannot help believing something gives another person no ground to believe the same thing, since it is a private argument.

There is no reason to think heart-based beliefs will be true, and the heart says different, even contradictory, things to different people (Russell's example: some savages' 'natural light' tells them it is their duty to eat people).

Even if the heart said the same thing to everyone, that would still be no evidence for the existence of anything beyond our own emotions -- desiring something, however intensely, is no ground for supposing it exists.
competing_positions: Traditional intellectual proofs of God's existence (ontological, cosmological, design arguments) offered by philosophers from Plato to Descartes and Leibniz, which Russell says at least could be refuted if invalid, unlike theology of the heart, which 'cannot be refuted, because it does not profess to prove its points.'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Accepted, in Russell's account, by the great majority of subsequent Protestant theologians as the standard mode of defending religious belief.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Shocked both Catholic and Protestant orthodoxy chiefly through its rejection of revelation and of eternal hell, and its claim that salvation is not confined to any one Church.

core_concepts.name: The Social Contract
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Rousseau's proposed solution to how people can unite into a society for mutual protection without losing their freedom: each person gives up all their rights completely and equally to the whole community, so that no one has power over anyone else specifically -- only the community as a whole, of which each person is an equal part, has authority.
core_concepts.precise_definition: 'The total alienation of each associate, together with all his rights, to the whole community,' forming 'a form of association which will defend and protect with the whole common force the person and goods of each associate, and in which each, while uniting himself with all, may still obey himself alone, and remain as free as before.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It reintroduced metaphysical abstraction into democratic theory and became, in Russell's account, 'the Bible of most of the leaders in the French Revolution', while its logic of total alienation to an indivisible collective made it available for use in defending totalitarian government.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Set out in The Social Contract (1762).
examples: 'The Sovereign, merely by virtue of what it is, is always what it should be.'
objections: If individuals retained any rights, there would be no common superior to judge disputes, so the theory demands total, reserve-less alienation -- which in Russell's reading amounts to 'a complete abrogation of liberty and a complete rejection of the doctrine of the rights of man.'

Rousseau's later softening (that the sovereign cannot impose useless fetters) is undercut because the sovereign alone judges what is useless, leaving 'only a very feeble obstacle... opposed to collective tyranny.'
competing_positions: Locke's social contract, which preserves individual rights (especially property) against the state and includes division of powers
Hobbes's absolutist contract, to which Russell says Rousseau's version is, on inspection, more akin
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Became foundational for revolutionary and later totalitarian political theory; Hegel is said to draw on Rousseau's misuse of the word 'freedom.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Denied the divine right of kings and advocated democracy, which along with its theological heterodoxy made it politically dangerous to the French government.

core_concepts.name: The General Will
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Not simply what most people happen to want (the 'will of all'), but the underlying common interest that would emerge if everyone's purely selfish, conflicting preferences cancelled each other out -- like how, in Russell's illustration, countless individual gravitational pulls in different directions cancel out to leave a single net pull toward the Earth's center.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The will belonging to the body politic as such, always right and always tending to the public advantage, distinct from both the will of the majority and the sum of individual wills (the 'will of all'); Rousseau holds it is best revealed when citizens deliberate without communicating or forming factions, so that 'the grand total of the small differences would always give the general will.'
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is, in Russell's words, 'both important and obscure,' and its vagueness is politically consequential: it allows whoever refuses to obey it to be 'forced to be free,' and it made possible, through its doctrine, 'the mystic identification of a leader with his people,' bypassing the need for confirmation by 'so mundane an apparatus as the ballot-box.'
core_concepts.historical_origin: Central concept of The Social Contract (1762).
examples: Russell's gravitational analogy: countless individual 'selfish' attractions among particles cancel out except for a net resultant pull toward Earth's center, fancifully conceivable as the Earth's 'general will'

Rousseau's claim that subordinate associations (churches, parties, trade unions) corrupt the general will by creating group interests, so the ideal (per Lycurgus, endorsed via Machiavelli) is a State with no partial societies at all
objections: Russell asks how, in practice, the general will's 'visible manifestations' are ever to be identified, since Rousseau 'leaves us in the dark.'

Applied to historical cases the concept becomes absurd or sinister: was Galileo 'forced to be free' when the Inquisition compelled his recantation because the 'general will' of the time was anti-Copernican? Is a criminal 'forced to be free' by imprisonment?
competing_positions: The 'will of all', i.e., the mere sum of individual, divergent self-interests, which Rousseau explicitly denies is the same as the general will
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell notes Hegel adopted Rousseau's paradoxical use of 'freedom' as essentially the right to obey the law/police, and credits Hegel with singling out the general-will/will-of-all distinction for praise.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Its logical consequence, if the state must eliminate 'partial societies,' is what Russell calls 'the Corporate or Totalitarian State, in which the individual citizen is powerless' -- churches, parties, and unions all being prohibited except a state church.

core_concepts.name: The state of nature and natural man
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Rousseau's hypothesis of an original human condition before civilization, in which 'natural man' is naturally good, self-sufficient, and at peace -- corrupted only later by the invention of private property and civil society.
core_concepts.precise_definition: A largely hypothetical original condition, admitted by Rousseau himself to be one 'which exists no longer, perhaps never existed, probably never will exist,' used as the baseline from which natural law and the origin of social inequality are deduced.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It grounds Rousseau's Discourse on Inequality (1754) and his central claim that 'man is naturally good, and only by institutions is he made bad' -- the direct antithesis of the Christian doctrine of original sin.
examples: 'The first man who, having enclosed a piece of land, bethought himself of saying "this is mine," and found people simple enough to believe him, was the real founder of civil society.'
Rousseau's claim that grain and metallurgy ('the symbol of our misfortune') introduced a 'deplorable revolution'
objections: Russell calls Rousseau's 'natural man' fictitious, not the savage known to anthropologists, yet somehow already a good husband and kind father with 'a religion of natural kindliness' -- more philosophically sophisticated than his supposed naïveté would allow.
competing_positions: The doctrine of original sin and salvation through the Church, which Rousseau's account of natural human goodness directly inverts
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Provides the basis for Rousseau's critique of civilization, private property, and inequality.

arguments.title: Rousseau's essay against the arts and sciences (Discourse of 1750)
premises: Science, letters, and the arts create artificial wants.
Chains (subjection) cannot be imposed on people who have no wants, as with naked American savages.
Therefore science, letters, and the arts are sources of slavery and the worst enemies of morals.

All the sciences, examined individually, have ignoble origins (astronomy from astrological superstition, eloquence from ambition, geometry from avarice, physics from vain curiosity, ethics from pride).
arguments.conclusion: Everything that distinguishes civilized man from the untutored barbarian is evil; science and virtue are incompatible.
arguments.explanation: Rousseau won the Academy of Dijon's prize with this essay in 1750 by defending the negative on the question of whether the arts and sciences had benefited humanity; Russell notes Rousseau then lived out its maxims, adopting a simple life and selling his watch.
objections: Voltaire's sardonic reply that reading the essay makes one 'long... to walk on all fours,' implying the argument's logical endpoint is an absurd rejection of all civilization Voltaire himself cannot literally adopt.
implications: Sets the pattern for Rousseau's later Discourse on Inequality and its critique of private property and civilization.

arguments.title: The fundamental problem of the Social Contract
premises: Individuals eventually can no longer maintain themselves in primitive independence and must unite for self-preservation.
Pledging one's liberty to a union appears to harm one's interests unless a special form of association can be found.
The required association must defend the person and goods of each member with the whole common force while still letting each 'obey himself alone, and remain as free as before.'
arguments.conclusion: The solution is total alienation of each associate, with all his rights, to the whole community -- since all give themselves absolutely and equally, no one has an interest in making the terms burdensome to others.
arguments.explanation: Russell walks through Rousseau's own statement of 'the fundamental problem of which the Social Contract provides the solution,' then shows that the demand for total, unreserved alienation removes any check against collective tyranny, since only a later, softer chapter admits (toothlessly) that the sovereign should not impose useless burdens.
objections: Total alienation without reserved individual rights implies 'a complete abrogation of liberty and a complete rejection of the doctrine of the rights of man,' per Russell.
The claim that the sovereign is 'always what it should be' is undercut by the fact that the sovereign, not any external body, is sole judge of what is useful to the community.
implications: Justifies, in Russell's reading, the totalitarian State -- a large field left open for despotic government even while nominally endorsing democracy.

arguments.title: Deriving the general will from cancelling self-interests
premises: Every citizen's political opinion is governed partly by an interest peculiar to himself and partly by an interest common to all members of the community.
If citizens deliberate without communicating or forming factions (log-rolling bargains), their divergent individual interests will tend to cancel out.
What remains after this cancellation is the interest common to all -- the resultant.
arguments.conclusion: This resultant is the general will, which is therefore always right, since it represents the largest collective satisfaction of self-interest possible to the community.
arguments.explanation: Russell offers his own interpretive reconstruction of Rousseau's obscure concept, illustrating it with the analogy of gravitational forces cancelling to leave a net pull toward the Earth's centre, and notes this is the best interpretation he could construct consistent with Rousseau's text.
objections: The practical identification of the general will remains undetermined: Rousseau's own conditions (no communication among citizens, no factions) are rarely met in practice, and subordinate associations (churches, parties, unions) are said to corrupt it -- pushing Rousseau toward prohibiting such associations altogether.
implications: If accepted literally, implies prohibiting all 'partial societies' within the State except possibly a state church, i.e., a Corporate/Totalitarian State.

key_distinctions: The 'general will' versus the 'will of all' (mere sum of individual wills)
The Sovereign (the community in its collective, legislative capacity) versus the government/executive (which may be tyrannical)
Rousseau's sense of 'democracy' (direct participation, as in the ancient City State) versus what we call democracy (which he terms 'elective aristocracy')
Liberty (Rousseau's nominal goal) versus equality (what Russell argues he actually values and pursues, even at liberty's expense)
Reason-based versus heart-based (feeling-based) justification of religious belief
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell contrasts Rousseau's theology of the heart with every prior philosopher from Plato through Descartes and Leibniz who offered intellectual proofs of God (excepting Pascal, whose 'the heart has its reasons, of which reason is ignorant' Russell calls 'quite in Rousseau's style'). Rousseau's Social Contract is compared point by point with Locke's (superficially similar, but substantively closer to Hobbes's) and contrasted with Locke's and Montesquieu's belief in division of powers and respect for private property.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell states flatly that Hitler is an outcome of Rousseau just as Roosevelt and Churchill are of Locke; that Hegel 'owed much to Rousseau' and adopted his paradoxical redefinition of 'freedom'; that Robespierre was Rousseau's 'faithful disciple' in theism and would have approved the Fête de l'Être Suprême; and that the Social Contract's mystique of the general will enabled later mystic identification of a leader with the people.
political_social_context: Rousseau's political writing emerged from, and was shaped by, his identity as 'citizen of Geneva' and his consequent preference for the small City State (on the Spartan/Lycurgan model, via Plutarch) over large territorial states like France and England; The Social Contract's rejection of the divine right of kings and its advocacy of democracy brought official condemnation from the French crown, the Sorbonne, the Parlement of Paris, and the Council of Geneva (which ordered his books burnt and his arrest).
religion_science_culture_context: Rousseau's own religious trajectory (Calvinist by birth, a Catholic convert in Turin, reconverted to Calvinism to regain Genevan citizenship) frames his invention of natural religion in 'The Confession of Faith of a Savoyard Vicar,' which Russell notes drew on Aristotle, Augustine, and Descartes despite professing to reject 'the wisdom of the philosophers.'
russell_presentation: Russell's presentation of Rousseau is pointedly two-sided and often openly hostile in tone toward the man while treating certain of his ideas as historically momentous. He opens by denying Rousseau was 'what would now be called a philosopher' at all, attributing his importance instead to his appeal to the heart and to sensibility, and spends roughly half the chapter on biographical material -- the Confessions, the theft blamed on an innocent maid, the abandonment of five children at the Foundling Hospital, the quarrels with Voltaire and the breach with Hume -- explicitly to explain his thought and influence rather than as mere gossip. Russell credits Rousseau with a genuine philosophical innovation (grounding religious belief in feeling rather than argument) while judging it, in his own voice, 'not... an advance,' and stating he would 'unhesitatingly choose' Aquinas over Rousseau if forced to pick. On the Social Contract, Russell reads a text that 'pays lip-service to democracy' as tending 'to the justification of the totalitarian State,' emphasizing that liberty is only Rousseau's nominal goal while equality is what he truly values, and tracing a direct line from Rousseau's doctrines to Robespierre, to Hegel's philosophy, and to the twentieth-century dictatorships of Russia and (especially) Germany.
critical_context: Common scholarly caveat: Russell's reading of Rousseau as proto-totalitarian, and his blunt equation 'Hitler is an outcome of Rousseau,' is a strongly polemical interpretation contested by many Rousseau scholars, who emphasize the 'general will' as a normative ideal of common good compatible with republican liberty rather than as a licence for despotism, and who read Rousseau's City-State preference and hostility to factions as continuous with classical republicanism (Sparta, Plutarch) rather than as anticipating twentieth-century totalitarian practice. Readers should treat Russell's causal chain from Rousseau to Robespierre to Hegel to Hitler as his own interpretive thesis, not an uncontested historical fact.
key_takeaways: Russell treats Rousseau primarily as a historically decisive 'social force' rather than as a rigorous philosopher, tracing his importance to his appeal to sensibility.

Rousseau invented the now-common Protestant strategy of grounding belief in God in feeling ('the heart') rather than in intellectual proof -- a move Russell considers historically original but philosophically indefensible.

The Social Contract calls for the total, unreserved alienation of individual rights to the community, which Russell reads as closer to Hobbes than to Locke and as opening the door to totalitarian government despite its democratic language.
The 'general will' is distinct from both the will of the majority and the mere sum of individual wills, but Rousseau never clearly explains how it can be identified in practice.
Rousseau's true priority, per Russell, is equality rather than liberty, even though liberty is his professed goal.

Russell draws a direct line of influence from Rousseau to Robespierre, to Hegel's misuse of 'freedom,' and to twentieth-century dictatorship, contrasting this lineage with the Lockean tradition he associates with liberal democracy.
study_notes:
This chapter works best read as two distinct arguments joined by one disreputable biography. First comes the theology: Rousseau's move from proof-based religion to feeling-based religion is genuinely original and enormously influential (Russell says most subsequent Protestant theology follows it), but Russell subjects it to a sharp two-part objection -- it is unreliable (no reason to think feelings track truth) and it is private (different hearts say different, even contradictory, things). Keep his 'rotten eggs' analogy in mind: suffering now is not evidence of blessedness later, any more than nine good dozen eggs are guaranteed by one bad dozen.

Second comes the political theory, which is the more historically consequential part of the chapter. Track three linked ideas carefully: (1) the social contract's demand for total alienation of rights, (2) the resulting concept of an infallible 'Sovereign' distinct from the (possibly tyrannical) government, and (3) the 'general will', which is supposed to guarantee the Sovereign's rightness but which Rousseau never operationalizes. Russell's gravitational analogy is a genuinely useful device for grasping the 'general will' concept even though he flags it as merely 'fanciful.' Notice how Rousseau's own text pulls in two directions: general, abstract principles that sound democratic, and detailed institutional prescriptions (hostility to factions, preference for small City States, near-elimination of intermediate associations) that push toward what Russell calls the Corporate or Totalitarian State.

Finally, be alert to Russell's evaluative framing throughout -- his biographical selections (the theft, the abandoned children, the persecution mania) are deployed to support his thesis that Rousseau's celebrated 'sensibility' substituted for, rather than reinforced, ordinary morality, and his closing historical claims (Hitler, Robespierre, Hegel) are his own strong interpretive judgments, not neutral historical consensus.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: A prized capacity for strong, spontaneous emotion, especially sympathy, that Rousseau's contemporaries valued highly and that Rousseau embodied and promoted despite his often unkind actions.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The eighteenth-century French cultural ideal of direct, uninformed emotional responsiveness that, per Russell, functioned in Rousseau's own ethic as a substitute for the ordinary virtues.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Rousseau's idea that people form society by each giving up all their individual rights completely and equally to the community as a whole, so no one person rules over another.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The total, unreserved alienation of each associate's person and rights to the whole community, creating a moral and collective body called the State (passive), the Sovereign (active), or a Power (in relation to other such bodies).

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The 'real' common interest of a community, different from just adding up what everyone individually wants, and always aimed at the public good.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The will belonging to the body politic as such, distinct from the will of the majority and from the 'will of all' (sum of individual wills); always tends to the public advantage, though Rousseau does not clearly specify how it is empirically identified.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Rousseau's paradoxical claim that making someone obey the general will, even against their own wishes, is actually making them free.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Rousseau's doctrine that whoever refuses to obey the general will 'shall be forced to do so,' which 'means nothing less than that he will be forced to be free' -- criticized by Russell as sophistical and later adopted, in modified form, by Hegel.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Rousseau's term for what we today call representative democracy (electing representatives), which he distinguishes from 'true' (direct) democracy.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Rousseau's classification of representative government as 'elective aristocracy' rather than democracy proper, since he reserves the term 'democracy' for direct participation of every citizen, as in the ancient City State.

questions.prompt: Why does Russell say Rousseau, despite not being 'what would now be called a philosopher', deserves a place in the history of philosophy?
questions.answer: Because of his immense influence as a social force -- as the father of the romantic movement, the initiator of systems that infer non-human facts from human emotion, and the inventor of the political philosophy of pseudo-democratic dictatorship.
questions.explanation: This is Russell's explicit justification for devoting a full chapter to a non-technical thinker.

questions.prompt: What is Rousseau's central theological innovation, according to Russell, and who does Russell say later adopted it?
questions.answer: Grounding belief in God on feeling (an aspect of human nature -- awe, conscience, aspiration) rather than on intellectual argument; Russell says this has since been accepted by the great majority of Protestant theologians.
questions.explanation: Russell treats this as Rousseau's most historically original philosophical contribution, distinct from his political theory.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Russell's two main objections to basing beliefs about objective fact on 'the heart.'
questions.answer: First, there is no reason to suppose such feeling-based beliefs will be true. Second, the resulting beliefs will be private and potentially contradictory, since the heart says different things to different people -- Russell's example being that some peoples' 'natural light' tells them cannibalism is a duty.
questions.explanation: These two objections form the backbone of Russell's critique of Rousseau's natural religion.

questions.prompt: Compare Rousseau's Social Contract to Locke's, as Russell presents the comparison.
questions.answer: Rousseau's contract at first seems analogous to Locke's but 'soon shows itself more akin to that of Hobbes': it demands total alienation of all rights to the community with no reserved individual rights, unlike Locke's contract, which preserves individual (especially property) rights and division of powers against the state.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this comparison to argue that Rousseau's language of freedom conceals an authoritarian substance.

questions.prompt: What does Rousseau mean by the 'general will', and what problem does Russell find with it?
questions.answer: The general will is the will of the body politic as such -- always right and tending to the common good, distinct from both majority rule and the mere sum of individual (self-interested) wills. Russell's problem is that Rousseau never explains how its 'visible manifestations' can actually be identified in practice.
questions.explanation: This distinction between the abstract concept and its practical unidentifiability is central to Russell's critique of Rousseau's political theory.

questions.prompt: Which philosopher does Russell say Hegel praised for distinguishing the general will from the will of all, and later 'owed much to' in political philosophy?
questions.explanation: Russell notes in a footnote that Hegel selects this distinction for special praise in his Logic, and elsewhere states Hegel adopted Rousseau's paradoxical redefinition of 'freedom.'

questions.prompt: According to Russell, does Rousseau ultimately value liberty or equality more, and what is the evidence?
questions.answer: Equality. Russell states that although liberty is the 'nominal goal' of Rousseau's thought, 'in fact it is equality that he values, and that he seeks to secure even at the expense of liberty,' as shown by the demand for total, equal alienation of rights in the Social Contract.
questions.explanation: This claim underlies Russell's broader argument that Rousseau's democratic rhetoric masks an authoritarian logic.

questions.prompt: What historical/political lineage does Russell trace from Rousseau, and to what rival lineage does he contrast it?
questions.answer: Russell traces Rousseau's influence through Robespierre and the Reign of Terror, through Hegel's defense of Prussian autocracy, to the twentieth-century dictatorships of Russia and (especially) Germany -- summed up in his claim 'Hitler is an outcome of Rousseau.' He contrasts this with the tradition descending from Locke, which he associates with Roosevelt and Churchill.
questions.explanation: This is one of Russell's most explicit and polemical historical claims in the chapter.

quiz.prompt: In what year(s) did Rousseau publish Emile and The Social Contract?
quiz.explanation: Russell states both Emile and The Social Contract appeared in 1762, the most fruitful year of Rousseau's productive period.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, whose tradition does he associate with Roosevelt and Churchill, in contrast to Rousseau's?
quiz.explanation: Russell writes: 'At the present time, Hitler is an outcome of Rousseau; Roosevelt and Churchill, of Locke.'

quiz.prompt: Russell claims that Rousseau was the first philosopher in history to offer any argument at all for God's existence.
quiz.explanation: False -- Russell says every philosopher before Rousseau who believed in God offered intellectual arguments; Rousseau's innovation was to ground belief in feeling instead.

quiz.prompt: Which historical figure does Russell single out as an exception among philosophers before Rousseau, on the grounds that 'the heart has its reasons, of which reason is ignorant' is 'quite in Rousseau's style'?
quiz.explanation: Russell notes this exception for Pascal in a footnote while discussing Rousseau's theological innovation.

quiz.prompt: In Russell's reconstruction, what happens to citizens' individual self-interests, according to Rousseau's account of how the general will emerges?
options: They are simply averaged by majority vote
Their divergent (selfish) parts cancel out, leaving a common resultant
They are abolished entirely by law
They are represented by an elected parliament
quiz.explanation: Russell compares this to gravitational forces cancelling out to leave a net pull toward the Earth's center, representing the common interest.

quiz.prompt: Rousseau's Social Contract opens with the famous line: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in ________.'
quiz.explanation: This is the opening rhetorical flourish of Book I of The Social Contract, quoted directly by Russell.

quiz.prompt: What does Rousseau term representative government, reserving the word 'democracy' for direct citizen participation as in the ancient City State?
quiz.explanation: Russell explains that when Rousseau speaks of democracy he means direct participation; representative government he calls 'elective aristocracy.'

quiz.prompt: Russell argues that Rousseau ultimately valued liberty more highly than equality, even in the Social Contract.
quiz.explanation: Russell argues the reverse: liberty is Rousseau's nominal goal, but 'in fact it is equality that he values, and that he seeks to secure even at the expense of liberty.'
